structuring.prompt: A large Indian private bank has seen its credit-card spends per card fall 15% over the last year while the number of cards grew. The head of cards asks you to find out why. Take a minute and lay out how you'd structure this problem. Tell me where you'd start.
structuring.reference: Strong structures are tailored: spend per card = share of active cards × spend per active card; spend per active card = transactions × ticket size, by segment (new vs old cards, channel of acquisition, customer segment) and category. Hypothesis: aggressive acquisition of new (lower-spend, often inactive) cards dilutes the average. The first branch should be 'new vs existing card mix' because the number of cards grew. Generic 'revenue/cost' or '4Ps' structures are weak here.

structuring.prompt: A state transport corporation's intercity bus occupancy has dropped from 78% to 61% in two years. Structure how you'd diagnose it.
structuring.reference: Demand vs supply: demand (total intercity travel on routes, the corporation's share vs private buses, rail, and own cars; by route and time) vs supply (seats added via new routes/frequency). Hypotheses: private operators on app platforms taking share on premium routes; new rail services; capacity added on weak routes. Strong answers prioritise checking whether seats offered changed (supply) before demand.

structuring.prompt: A global paint company wants to know whether to launch a waterproofing product line in India. How would you structure your analysis?
structuring.reference: Tailored to the decision: market attractiveness (size, growth, profitability of waterproofing, segments like roofs/walls/bathrooms, channels via contractors and dealers), ability to win (brand, dealer network overlap, applicator/contractor influence, technology), economics (margins, investment, payback), and entry mode (build vs acquire). Strong answers note that contractors/applicators drive the purchase decision, which changes the go-to-market.

structuring.prompt: An edtech company's offline tuition centres are losing money while its online courses are profitable. The CEO asks whether to shut the centres. Give me your structure.
structuring.reference: Decision-focused structure: centre-level economics (revenue per centre = students × fees; costs = rent, faculty, marketing) by centre segment; strategic role of centres (do centres feed online sales, brand trust, conversion?); options (shut, fix, franchise, hybrid). Key: check cross-effects before shutting. A generic profitability tree that ignores the online-offline link is weak.

structuring.prompt: A hospital chain wants to cut its average patient waiting time in outpatient departments from 90 minutes to 30. Structure the problem.
structuring.reference: Process/journey structure: registration → triage/vitals → wait for doctor → consultation → diagnostics → pharmacy/billing. For each step: demand arrival pattern vs capacity (staff, rooms), process time, and variability/scheduling. Hypothesis: arrival peaks (everyone comes at 9-11 am) and doctor late starts drive most of the wait. Good answers are MECE along the journey and prioritise by where time is lost.

structuring.prompt: A mid-sized cement company's profit margins are well below the industry average even though its plants are relatively new. How would you structure this?
structuring.reference: Margin gap vs peers: price realisation (region/market mix, brand, trade vs non-trade) and cost per tonne (power & fuel, raw materials, freight/logistics — a major cost in cement given lead distance, overheads). Hypothesis: new plants often mean long lead distances to markets, so freight is higher; or they sell in oversupplied regions. Prioritise freight and realisation over plant efficiency since plants are new.

prioritization.prompt: You're working on a case about a D2C mattress brand whose profits fell 40%. You've laid out: (1) revenue: volume, price, mix; (2) costs: raw materials (foam prices up 25% industry-wide), logistics, marketing (CAC up 60%), returns (return rate flat). You have 10 minutes with the client CFO. Which two branches do you investigate first, and why?
prioritization.reference: Prioritise by likely size and evidence: marketing/CAC (up 60%, D2C economics are marketing-heavy) and raw materials (foam +25%, a large share of COGS). Also ask whether prices were raised to offset foam. Returns are flat, so deprioritise. The strong answer states the hypothesis and the data needed to confirm it.

prioritization.prompt: A client's national chain of optical stores wants to grow revenue 30% next year. Options on the table: open 40 new stores, launch eye tests at home, start selling contact lenses online, raise prices on premium frames, add hearing aids. You can only pursue two. Which, and why?
prioritization.reference: Criteria: size of impact within one year, time to implement, investment, fit with capabilities, risk. Likely: new stores (proven, but capex and ramp-up time) and online contact lenses (recurring, low capex, existing customer base). Price increases are fast but small; hearing aids are a new category with regulation and fit risk. A strong answer states explicit criteria and a rough size for each.

prioritization.prompt: In a case about falling sales at a snack company, you learn: sales down 12%; the category grew 6%; two competitors launched cheaper packs; your distribution in rural stores fell from 55% to 48%; ad spend flat. Where do you go first and why?
prioritization.reference: Share loss (category +6% vs -12%) → two candidates: competitive price packs and rural distribution loss. Rural distribution dropped 7 points, a large, measurable, controllable driver; start there and check the sales split urban vs rural. Price packs are a second check. The strong answer notes the category is growing, so it's a share problem, not a market problem.

prioritization.prompt: You're advising a city hospital on reducing cancelled surgeries. Causes found: patients not medically ready on the day (35%), no ICU bed available (25%), surgeon unavailable (20%), missing consent/paperwork (10%), other (10%). You can launch one initiative this quarter. Which one?
prioritization.reference: Consider impact × ease: pre-op readiness clinic addresses 35% and is operationally simple; ICU bed availability (25%) needs capacity/scheduling changes (harder). Paperwork is easy but small. Strong answer: pre-op readiness clinic first, with an explicit impact/ease reasoning and a follow-up on ICU bed scheduling.

prioritization.prompt: An airline-catering company has four issues: late deliveries to aircraft (8% of flights), food waste at 18% of production, a contract up for renewal with its largest customer in 6 months, and rising staff attrition (30%). The CEO asks where to focus first. What do you say?
prioritization.reference: The largest customer contract renewal in 6 months is existential and time-bound. Late deliveries directly affect that relationship (on-time performance is a key KPI for airlines), so tie them together. Waste is a margin issue; attrition may drive both. Strong answers prioritise by consequence and urgency and link issues rather than listing them.

hypothesis.prompt: A popular South Indian restaurant chain's same-store sales are down 10% this year, but footfall is flat. State your initial hypothesis and what data you'd ask for to test it.
hypothesis.reference: Flat footfall + lower sales → average bill per customer fell. Hypotheses: menu/price changes, shift in mix toward cheaper items, lower party size, more solo lunch traffic, discounting on aggregator orders. Data: average bill trend, items per bill, party size, channel mix (dine-in vs delivery), discount levels. Strong answers state a specific, falsifiable hypothesis.

hypothesis.prompt: A two-wheeler maker's sales in rural India dropped 20% while urban sales grew 5%. What's your hypothesis?
hypothesis.reference: Rural-specific demand shock: poor monsoon/farm incomes, tighter rural financing (NBFC credit tightening), or price increases from regulatory costs (e.g., new safety/emission norms) hurting price-sensitive rural buyers. Strong candidates pick one leading hypothesis, justify it, and say how to test (e.g., sales by district vs rainfall; financing approval rates).

hypothesis.prompt: A pharma company's new diabetes drug has had strong doctor awareness in surveys but prescriptions are 60% below forecast after one year. What do you think is going on?
hypothesis.reference: Awareness is not the issue; barriers after awareness: price/affordability vs generics, insurance/formulary inclusion in hospitals, availability at chemists (distribution), side effects/perceived efficacy, or patients dropping off refills. Strong answer: 'I think it's affordability relative to established generics, because diabetes is chronic and patients are price-sensitive' + test with prescriptions vs refills and by channel.

hypothesis.prompt: A SaaS company's customer support costs doubled in a year while customers grew 20%. What's your initial hypothesis?
hypothesis.reference: Costs growing much faster than customers → tickets per customer or cost per ticket rose. Hypothesis: a product change/release increased tickets per customer, or new customer segments (smaller, less tech-savvy) need more support; or staffing moved to more expensive support. Test: tickets per customer by cohort and ticket category after releases.

synthesis.prompt:
Here's what we found for a regional supermarket chain that's losing money:
- Revenue flat for 3 years; footfall down 8%, average bill up 8%
- Fresh produce wastage is 14% vs 6% for competitors
- 5 of 32 stores make 70% of losses; all opened in the last 2 years in new suburbs
- Online orders via aggregators are 9% of revenue at a -3% margin

The CEO walks in. Give me your 30-second synthesis and recommendation.
synthesis.reference: Lead with the answer: losses are concentrated in 5 new suburban stores and in fresh wastage; online via aggregators is loss-making at small scale. Recommendation: fix or close the 5 new stores (review catchment, cut size/costs, exit if no path in 6 months), cut fresh wastage to ~6% (demand forecasting, smaller replenishment, markdowns), and renegotiate or cap aggregator orders. Data → insight → implication → action. Reciting the bullets back is weak.

synthesis.prompt:
Findings for a fintech lending app:
- Loan book grew 80% last year
- 90-day default rate rose from 3% to 7%, concentrated in customers acquired via a new partner channel
- That channel brings 40% of new loans at half the acquisition cost
- Interest rates can't be raised due to regulatory caps

Synthesise for the board in under a minute.
synthesis.reference: Answer first: growth is being bought through a cheap channel that brings much riskier borrowers, and at capped rates the extra defaults likely wipe out the acquisition savings. Recommendation: tighten underwriting for that channel immediately (or pause it), reprice the partnership (risk-sharing/first-loss guarantee), and track cohort-level losses. Data → insight → implication → action, with the economic trade-off explicit.

synthesis.prompt:
Findings for an FMCG company's new premium shampoo:
- Trial is strong: 22% of target households tried it in 6 months
- Repeat purchase is 12% vs 35% category norm
- Consumer feedback: 'nice fragrance, didn't see a difference, too expensive for daily use'
- Distribution reached 80% of planned stores

What do you tell the brand head?
synthesis.reference: The launch has a repeat problem, not an awareness or distribution problem: people try it but don't come back because they don't see enough benefit for the price. Implication: more marketing spend would buy more one-off trials. Action: either strengthen the product benefit (visible result) or reposition/price for occasional use (smaller packs, sachets) and test before scaling spend.

synthesis.prompt:
In a market entry case for a Japanese air-conditioner brand entering India you found:
- Indian room AC market ~1.1 crore units a year, growing 12%
- Top 3 brands have 55% share; strong dealer relationships and service networks
- Consumers rank after-sales service as the #2 purchase criterion after price
- The client has no service network in India; building one takes ~3 years

Synthesise and recommend.
synthesis.reference: Attractive market but the barrier is after-sales service, which consumers value highly and incumbents own. Implication: a standalone entry would struggle for 3 years. Action: enter via a partnership/JV or acquisition that brings a service network (or contract with a third-party service provider), start in a few regions, then scale. The answer links the finding to the entry mode.

clarification.prompt: Here's a case opening: 'Our client is a telecom company and its profits are down. What should it do?' What clarifying questions would you ask before structuring? Keep it to the ones that matter.
clarification.reference: Good clarifications: which business (mobile/broadband/enterprise) and geography; time frame and magnitude of decline; the objective and any target; whether the whole industry is affected; any recent changes (pricing, regulation, spectrum costs). Poor: asking for data that belongs in analysis (full cost breakdown) or too many questions. 3-5 sharp questions is the norm.

clarification.prompt: Case opening: 'A private university wants to double its student intake. Should it?' What would you clarify first?
clarification.reference: Objective (revenue? reputation? mission?), time frame, which programmes, current capacity/utilisation (seats, faculty, hostels), constraints (regulatory approvals, accreditation), and what 'should it' is judged on (profitability, quality). Strong answers clarify the objective and constraints first.

clarification.prompt: Guesstimate: 'Estimate the number of smartphones sold in India per year.' What would you clarify before starting?
clarification.reference: Scope: new units only or including refurbished/second-hand; all price bands; units vs value; B2C only or including enterprise; the year. Keep it short: 2-3 questions. Strong answers also say why it matters (e.g., refurbished could be a large share).

clarification.prompt: Case opening: 'Our client is a global logistics firm considering acquiring an Indian warehousing company.' What do you ask?
clarification.reference: Why (strategic rationale: capability, market access, capacity), what success looks like (returns, timelines), deal size/constraints, the target's profile (size, locations, customers), and whether there are alternatives being considered. Avoid jumping to financial details prematurely.

exhibit.prompt: A consumer electronics retailer shares this chart. Take a look. What stands out to you, and what would you ask next?
exhibit.reference: Revenue grows every year but gross margin falls steadily from 22% to 14%, and the share of revenue from smartphones (low-margin) grows from 30% to 55%. So growth is mix-driven toward low-margin categories and the margin decline is a mix effect. Next: margin by category, and whether accessories/services attach rates fell.

exhibit.title: Retailer revenue, gross margin and category mix

exhibit.prompt: Here's data from a food delivery company's operations in one city. What stands out?
exhibit.reference: Delivery time jumps sharply in the 8-10 pm peak (38 → 52 minutes) while order volume peaks, and cancellation rate triples at peak. Riders online don't scale with orders at peak (orders per rider rise from ~1.4 to ~2.6). Implication: rider supply at peak is the bottleneck, driving cancellations; look at peak incentives or batching.

exhibit.title: One city: orders, riders and service by time band

exhibit.prompt: A coaching institute shows you this. What's the story?
exhibit.reference: Enquiries grew strongly but conversion from enquiry to enrolment collapsed (from 25% to ~11%), so enrolments are flat. The problem is conversion, not lead generation; likely lower lead quality from new digital channels or pricing/competition. Next: conversion by lead source.

exhibit.prompt: An electric scooter maker shows you warranty claims data. What stands out?
exhibit.reference: Claims are concentrated in batteries and in scooters made in Q3 at Plant B (a spike from ~2% to ~7%), while other components are stable. Implication: a batch/supplier quality issue at Plant B in Q3, not a design issue across the fleet; next check the battery cell supplier/lot for that period and consider a targeted recall.

exhibit.title: Warranty claims rate by production quarter and plant (% of units)
exhibit.unit: % of units with a battery warranty claim
